generalizedRange: Hawaiʻi — bred in care, returning to Maui's forests
hook: Extinct in the wild since 2002. Five now fly over Maui.

story.text: The ʻalalā is Hawaiʻi's largest surviving forest bird: a soft-black crow with brownish wings and stiff throat feathers it raises in display.
It speaks in at least 34 distinct calls — shrieks, howls, whoops, and cries that sound almost human.
It was the forest's gardener, carrying and planting the seeds of native trees.
In 2002 the last wild birds were gone, and the species was declared extinct in the wild.
It survived indoors: from fewer than twenty birds in the late 1990s, conservation breeding has grown the flock past one hundred and ten.
Wildness is harder to restore than numbers. Releases on Hawaiʻi Island struggled, in part because the ʻio — the Hawaiian hawk — was waiting.
So in late 2024 the project tried a new island: five juveniles flew free in East Maui, where no ʻio live.
They wear GPS backpacks and visit feeder boxes while they learn to be wild.
In Hawaiian culture the ʻalalā are ʻaumākua — spirit guardians. Like our ancestors, a recovery specialist says: the forest wouldn't be there without these birds.
To witness the ʻalalā is to hold a door open — e hoʻolāʻau hou ka ʻalalā: may it thrive in its forest once again.

reproduction.text: Pairs mate for life. One to five greenish-blue eggs come between March and July, incubated by the female for three weeks; usually two chicks survive. Since 1996, breeding centers on two islands have carried the species.

insight.text: A 2016 study showed the ʻalalā naturally makes and uses stick tools — among crows, a talent shared only with the New Caledonian crow.
